rv.q: The warmth generated by the pair fills the Troubadour's rather daunting space and their voices blend beautifully, diffusing the memory of the brash, boisterous opening numbers and continual scene-setting.
Even the most casual viewers will find something to love in this visually enthralling production.

No, it can't escape the limitations of the story's spectacularly two-dimensional characters, who are siloed into the camps of jock, brainiac or drama kid, and whose stock traits are indulged in the book by David Simpatico, but it's bright and buzzy nonetheless.

Despite the school pinning its hopes of athletic success on him, and the mathletes hoping Gabriella can bring them a trophy, the pair is also intrigued by the arts, auditioning together for a part in the school’s musical. Should they stick to their designated roles, or shoot for something new together?
The result is an absolute slam dunk, capturing everything audiences loved about the original while finding fresh energy of its own.
The result is a sweet, warm and humorous story with a great message that should continue to inspire audiences, encouraging them to follow their heart’s desires.
It’s simply a fun, feel-good stage adaptation that gives fans another chance to enjoy the songs and characters they grew up with.

You could genuinely revitalise me from a coma with the opening notes of I've Had the Time of My Life or the first bars of Don't You (Forget About Me). So, naturally, High School Musical is right up my street. This is feel-good theatre with the stakes pleasingly low.

High School Musical soars and flies, particularly with its ambitious choreography and ensemble pieces. Reimagined by Aaron Renfree, Get’Cha Head in the Game almost defies belief with the smart basketball choreography, whilst Stick to the Status Quo satisfies with staging detail and We’re All in This Together is infectiously energetic.

cn.t: This nostalgic stage adaptation captures the earnest, squeaky-clean energy of Disney's beloved film with catchy songs and boisterous performances, though its painstakingly wholesome approach may feel dated to modern audiences.
